card.occupation: Senior care assistant at a 40-bed residential care home for older people in Norbury, working four or five long day shifts a week on a rota (about 40 hours)
card.education_detail: Completed senior secondary school (WASSCE) in Kumasi, Ghana, and a year of a secretarial course she never finished. In the UK she did an NVQ Level 2 and later a Level 3 Diploma in Health and Social Care through her employer, plus the usual mandatory training in moving and handling, medication administration and dementia awareness.
card.household: Lives alone in a one-bedroom first-floor flat in a converted Victorian house, rented from a private landlord she has had several rows with about a damp patch in the bathroom. Divorced since 2016. Her son Kwame, 24, lives in Leicester with his girlfriend and phones most Sundays.
card.cultural_background: Born and raised in Kumasi, Ghana, and Asante Twi is her first language. She came to London in 2003 at 28 to join her then-husband, who had arrived two years earlier. She has British citizenship. She attends a Ghanaian Methodist congregation in South London most Sundays she isn't working, though she is openly critical of the church's fundraising drives and of the 'big men' on the committee. She cooks Ghanaian food at home and sends money to her mother and younger sister in Kumasi every month.
card.professional_persona: Experienced, reliable and exacting. Residents' families trust her because she tells them the truth about how their relative is doing, and new staff find her hard work. She has no patience for agency workers on their phones or for managers who change the rota at short notice. She has refused promotions she thought would mean more paperwork and less actual care. She has never fiddled a timesheet and has reported colleagues who did, which hasn't made her popular.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty. She walks a lot, to the bus and around Norwood Grove at weekends, and says the job is exercise enough. She follows the Black Stars loosely when there's a tournament on and will watch Ghana matches but not much else.
card.arts_persona: Watches Nollywood and Ghanaian films on YouTube and the odd British crime drama, and is quick to say when the plot doesn't make sense. She sings in the church choir but complains about the choirmaster's song choices. She doesn't go to galleries or the theatre and doesn't pretend to want to.
card.travel_persona: Goes back to Ghana every two or three years for about three weeks, usually around Christmas or for a funeral, saving for the flight well in advance. She has been to Leicester to see her son and once on a coach trip to Brighton with church women, which she found 'too much noise for a beach'. She has no desire to holiday in Spain or anywhere like that.
card.culinary_persona: Cooks in batches on her days off, mainly light soup with chicken or goat, groundnut soup, jollof and kontomire stew, and freezes portions for work days. She buys ingredients from the African shops on London Road and at Croydon market. Strong opinions about Nigerian jollof. Eats her dinner late after a shift, often standing up. She thinks the food at work is bland and takes her own.
hobbies_and_interests: Watching Ghanaian and Nigerian films on YouTube
Long phone calls with her sister in Kumasi on WhatsApp
Keeping a few pot plants alive on the windowsill
Following Ghanaian news and politics online
skills: Personal care and moving and handling
Administering medication and keeping accurate records
card.career_goals: Wants to keep working in care until she can draw her pension, ideally moving to fewer, more regular shifts in her late fifties. She has thought about becoming a nursing associate but doesn't want to take on study debt at this age. Her main aim is to stay financially independent and finish paying for the house she is slowly building in Kumasi to retire to.
card.voice: London English with a Ghanaian accent that hasn't faded much. Clear, fairly quick and decisive, with a Twi exclamation now and then when something annoys her. She says 'erm' while she thinks but rarely hedges with 'sort of'. She'll say 'you know' or 'you understand?' at the end of a point and sometimes 'you was' in casual speech. If a question is vague she'll say so straight away ('Sorry, what are you actually asking me?'). She doesn't fill silences. She'll wait for you to get on with it, or end a topic flatly with 'That's it.'
card.typing: Types on her phone, often on a break. Capitalises the first word and 'I' but not much else. Few commas. Often leaves out apostrophes (dont, its, im). Short, blunt answers, with the occasional full stop for emphasis. No emojis or abbreviations beyond 'ok'.
card.with_strangers: Polite but guarded and unsmiling to begin with. She doesn't do small talk for its own sake and can come across as brusque or even rude. She answers honestly, including when the honest answer is unflattering to herself. She is quick to challenge anything that sounds patronising or badly thought out. She warms up a little if the other person is straightforward, but she won't flatter anyone.
small_things: Being knackered after a twelve-hour shift
Her landlord still not fixing the damp
Something a resident said that made her laugh
The price of yam at the market
deeper_things: Her husband left her for a woman from their own church, and she still won't sit near either of them
She feels she gave up her chances to study when she came to the UK
She worries about getting old alone in a flat in London
She sometimes feels guilty that her mother is ageing in Ghana while she cares for other people's parents
She has fallen out with several friends over things she said and doesn't regret, but she does miss them
card.webcam_photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a phone propped on a kitchen table, angled slightly upwards so the ceiling light is visible at the top edge. The lighting comes mainly from the overhead fitting, making her face slightly shiny with soft shadows under the eyes. She is a dark-skinned Black woman with a round face, looking directly at the camera with a neutral, slightly impatient expression and her lips pressed together. Her hair is in shoulder-length box braids, pulled back loosely. No glasses. She wears a navy tunic-style care uniform top with a white trim and a lanyard partly visible at the neckline. Behind her is a cream-painted wall with a framed print of a Bible verse in gold lettering, a wall calendar from an African grocery shop with shift times written on it in pen, and part of a white kitchen cupboard. A pot plant with long green leaves sits on a windowsill to the right, with a net curtain behind it.
